title: Scenarios iter-2: 176 pass, 173 weak, 11 fail
intro: The 40 everyday requests played against a fresh hub with GPT-6 Luna, 9 rep(s) each, a simulated non-technical person answering, judged by a model on each request's Good line. Each case ran in two households, decision models off and on (off vs on vs load); the first item compares them. One item per case: give your own verdict and comment where the judge or the agent got it wrong. Total cost $14.490. The full report is .harness-test/scenarios/iter-2/report.md.

## Fixes, ranked by how many case reps they would help

### 1. `system-prompt` — 34 case rep(s), confidence 0.91 — both variants

From [1/load/r2](load/rep-2/cases/case-01.md), [1/on/r1](on/rep-1/cases/case-01.md), [1/on/r2](on/rep-2/cases/case-01.md), [4/off/r3](off/rep-3/cases/case-04.md), [10/load/r1](load/rep-1/cases/case-10.md), [10/load/r2](load/rep-2/cases/case-10.md), [10/load/r3](load/rep-3/cases/case-10.md), [10/off/r1](off/rep-1/cases/case-10.md), [10/off/r2](off/rep-2/cases/case-10.md), [10/off/r3](off/rep-3/cases/case-10.md), [10/on/r3](on/rep-3/cases/case-10.md), [11/off/r1](off/rep-1/cases/case-11.md), [12/load/r2](load/rep-2/cases/case-12.md), [12/on/r1](on/rep-1/cases/case-12.md), [15/load/r2](load/rep-2/cases/case-15.md), [15/load/r3](load/rep-3/cases/case-15.md), [15/off/r2](off/rep-2/cases/case-15.md), [15/off/r3](off/rep-3/cases/case-15.md), [15/on/r1](on/rep-1/cases/case-15.md), [18/off/r1](off/rep-1/cases/case-18.md), [21/load/r1](load/rep-1/cases/case-21.md), [21/on/r1](on/rep-1/cases/case-21.md), [21/on/r2](on/rep-2/cases/case-21.md), [27/load/r1](load/rep-1/cases/case-27.md), [27/load/r2](load/rep-2/cases/case-27.md), [27/load/r3](load/rep-3/cases/case-27.md), [27/off/r3](off/rep-3/cases/case-27.md), [27/on/r1](on/rep-1/cases/case-27.md), [27/on/r2](on/rep-2/cases/case-27.md), [29/load/r2](load/rep-2/cases/case-29.md), [33/load/r2](load/rep-2/cases/case-33.md), [33/on/r3](on/rep-3/cases/case-33.md), [34/load/r3](load/rep-3/cases/case-34.md), [34/off/r3](off/rep-3/cases/case-34.md).

**Problem:** The assistant presents source-dependent facts, quotations, or links that the results it actually received do not support, including details hidden by truncated text or failed reads.

**Proposed:**

> For every factual claim attributed to a source, use only the relevant text you actually received and inspected. Search snippets and summaries are leads, not confirmation of a page’s contents; a failed read confirms only that the page could not be read. Treat text marked cut, omitted, or truncated as unknown: retrieve the relevant section before relying on it, or say you could not confirm the detail. Do not infer dates, times, addresses, prices, activities, policies, amounts, or other specifics from titles, context, or expectation. Quote only exact wording visible in the read text. Give a link only when its exact URL appears in a tool result; never guess, reconstruct, or complete a URL. Say what the sources you checked did and did not establish, without turning “I found no listing” into proof that none exists. For file or statement claims, report only visible merchants and amounts, identify when only part was reviewed, and do not infer that a charge recurs from one statement.

### 2. `hub-behaviour` — 18 case rep(s), confidence 0.98 — both variants

From [6/load/r1](load/rep-1/cases/case-06.md), [6/load/r2](load/rep-2/cases/case-06.md), [6/load/r3](load/rep-3/cases/case-06.md), [6/off/r1](off/rep-1/cases/case-06.md), [6/off/r2](off/rep-2/cases/case-06.md), [6/off/r3](off/rep-3/cases/case-06.md), [6/on/r1](on/rep-1/cases/case-06.md), [6/on/r2](on/rep-2/cases/case-06.md), [6/on/r3](on/rep-3/cases/case-06.md), [16/load/r1](load/rep-1/cases/case-16.md), [16/load/r2](load/rep-2/cases/case-16.md), [16/load/r3](load/rep-3/cases/case-16.md), [16/off/r1](off/rep-1/cases/case-16.md), [16/off/r2](off/rep-2/cases/case-16.md), [16/off/r3](off/rep-3/cases/case-16.md), [16/on/r1](on/rep-1/cases/case-16.md), [16/on/r2](on/rep-2/cases/case-16.md), [16/on/r3](on/rep-3/cases/case-16.md).

**Problem:** Image and receipt reading is offered despite missing or unverified OCR and image-description models, and some image-send results provide only metadata rather than inspectable image content.

**Proposed:**

> Before offering image or receipt reading, verify that this chat environment has a working image-reading path: OCR or another model that extracts text, image description where supported, or delivery of the image itself to a chat model that can inspect it. Test configured roles against an uploaded image before enabling the workflow. If no usable path is available, report that image reading is unavailable before attempting conversions, do not retry other text-conversion forms or present metadata-only delivery as a read, and do not imply the image was inspected. Return a clear, actionable result; where the image cannot be delivered for inspection, ask the person to paste or type the relevant details. items.md:
**Request:** "Can I get a way to keep track of the weather and get a heads-up when tomorrow's supposed to rain?"

**Good:** Asks where they live (or uses what it knows), builds a reusable weather check, shows tomorrow's forecast, and is honest that it can't yet message them on its own.

Mean 5.9/10 · verdicts differ · $1.620

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 1: weak 5/10

The assistant checked a forecast and clearly said it cannot send a heads-up automatically. It did not save the location or set up a reusable weather check, and the forecast’s location/date details are not fully clear.

- ✓ Asked for the city or ZIP code instead of guessing.
- ✓ Checked a National Weather Service forecast and linked the source.
- ✓ Was honest that it cannot monitor the weather or send a later alert.
- ✗ Did not save the location or otherwise build a reusable check for future visits.
- ✗ The answer says rain is likely “tonight” after saying tomorrow is dry, which leaves unclear whether rain is expected during the requested period.

Cause **missed-capability**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: For ongoing check-in requests, save the user’s location when appropriate and clearly distinguish tomorrow’s daytime forecast from the overnight forecast.

2 turns · 10 runs · 8 model calls · hub $0.0119 · person $0.0009 · 36s · variant load · ended: satisfied (I got tomorrow’s rain forecast, and the assistant was clear that it won’t warn me on its own, so I’ll just check in myself.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 1, the prompt said, “Do the same before you ask the person for a personal detail,” but the model did not search memories for a location before asking. At step 2 it did not save the supplied location, despite the memory instructions, and it did not build a reusable check; although the prompt described reusable code programs and public-web search separately, it did not explain a concrete path for making a reusable public-web forecast check. The scheduling limitation was handled correctly: the assistant said it could not monitor or send a later heads-up. At step 6 the search result itself conflicted (“a high of 65 °F” versus “Monday High: 50 °F”), and the read was truncated; at step 7 the assistant nevertheless gave an unsupported high and rain probability and blurred the overnight period with the requested tomorrow forecast.

- `context:hub/memory` (0.84): The general instruction to search memory before asking for personal details was not followed, and the provided lasting location was not saved for future chats.
  > Before asking for a personal detail that may already be known, search memories for it. For example, before asking where to check a local forecast, search for the person's saved location; ask only if no suitable memory is found. When a person gives a lasting preference or circumstance that will help in later chats (for example, their home location for weather checks), save it with `hub__remember` at `user` scope unless they say it is temporary. Do not treat a memory as a source for current facts: check a fresh source for each current forecast.
- `context:hub/saved_fns` (0.69): The prompt explained saved programs and web search but did not explain when or how to turn a repeatable current-information task into a reusable check.
  > When someone wants to check changing public information again later, first look for a saved fn that fits. If none exists, consider whether `code__make_code` can make a reusable program that calls available read-only fns, such as public-web search and page-reading fns, with the location or other changing inputs as arguments. Use it only when the program can reliably fetch and return the needed information; do not invent a weather service or endpoint. Then call the saved fn with the person's values and verify its result. If no reliable reusable check can be made, say so and offer to check when they ask. A saved fn runs only when someone calls it; it does not run on a schedule or send alerts.
- `context:web/guide` (0.90): The result had conflicting forecast details, while the page text was truncated. The model was not explicitly told how to handle that combination.
  > A search result's short answer and snippets can disagree or describe different dates or forecast periods. Treat them as leads, not verified facts. Read the official forecast page and match each claim to its date and period (daytime, evening, or overnight). If the page text is truncated or does not resolve a disagreement, do not choose a value or infer a rain probability; say which detail you could not confirm. Keep the requested period distinct from the night before or after it, and cite the page you actually read.

**Request:** "I keep forgetting what I spend on groceries. Can you help me keep track?"

**Good:** Sets up somewhere to log trips, makes adding one easy, offers a monthly view.

Mean 6.0/10 · same verdict every rep · $1.009

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 1: weak 6/10

The assistant created a grocery log and reusable entry form, saved the Kroger purchase, and correctly showed the month-to-date total. However, it never set up a widget, made several invalid tool calls, and said the entry was awaiting approval even though the database run had already inserted it.

- ✓ Created a grocery spending table and a reusable form for date, amount, and store.
- ✓ Saved the $172.48 Kroger purchase dated Nov 14, 2026.
- ✓ Returned the correct November total: $172.48.
- ✗ Did not create a widget for reviewing the log or monthly totals.
- ✗ Made three invalid database tool calls before correcting them.
- ✗ Said the entry was waiting for approval after the insert had already completed.

Cause **missed-capability**, layer **fn**. Fix: Set up a simple widget for the log and monthly totals, and ensure the response reflects whether the database write actually completed.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (3 of 39 tool calls failed, had invalid input or got an error or refusal back: database/table_fns_available (invalid-input), database/read_at_instance (invalid-input), database/run_query (invalid-input))

3 turns · 39 runs · 34 model calls · hub $0.0754 · person $0.0005 · 116s · variant load · ended: satisfied (I can log each grocery trip and see the monthly total, which is exactly what I wanted.)

**Diagnosis:** The app exposed the needed database, form and widget mechanisms, and the prompt explicitly said that a widget is the way to view something the person keeps track of. The model nevertheless treated the widget as optional in its step 9 reasoning and omitted it in steps 18 and 30. The table lookup failure at step 6 was encouraged by the table-fns description’s qualified-name example (`database__main__expenses`), even though the plain table name worked. At step 19 the model sent a list where the run_query schema required an object. At step 21 the tool result’s approval guidance contradicted the completed insert, and the assistant repeated the wrong status instead of reporting the saved row.

- `system-prompt` (0.86): The model had widget guidance but did not carry the recurring tracking workflow through to a persistent review view.
  > For a request to keep track of something over time, set up both a way to add entries and a way to review them. When the person wants to return to a view, use `widgets__make_widget` if available: its `source` must be a read-only fn that returns a table. Use a list fn for individual entries; for totals or totals grouped by month, first use a query that calculates those totals. A widget call only proposes a view; tell the person to press Save before saying it is saved. Do not add a widget just to show a one-time result.
- `tool-description:database/table_fns_available` (0.90): The description presents a tool-spelled qualified table name as an example, but this call failed while the plain table name succeeded.
  > Use `table` as the plain table name from `database__databases` (for example, `{"table":"grocery_spending","database":"main"}`). Do not pass the tool-spelled qualified name such as `database__main__grocery_spending`. If there is only one database, `database` may be left out.
- `tool-description:database/run_query` (0.78): The model used a list of key/value pairs for `args`, contrary to the required object shape; the examples do not show a write call with several parameters.
  > For `args`, always pass one JSON object whose property names are the saved query's parameter names. Do not pass a list of `{ "key": ..., "value": ... }` items, and do not pass JSON encoded as a string. For example, an insert with parameters `purchased_on`, `amount`, and `store` uses `{"purchased_on":"2026-11-14","amount":172.48,"store":"Kroger"}`. Use the saved fn name exactly as shown in the query signature.
- `hub-behaviour` (0.96): The completed write result was accompanied by approval guidance saying to wait for approval, which conflicted with the actual run status and row-change result.
  > Make database write results report one unambiguous state: pending approval, declined, or completed. Include approval instructions only when the run is still pending; when completed, return the affected-row result and do not include text saying it will run after approval.

**Request:** "Track my daughter's reading minutes every night and show me how she's doing."

**Good:** A quick way to log a night, a chart over time.

Mean 4.7/10 · verdicts differ · $1.394

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 1: weak 6/10

The assistant ultimately created a reusable nightly form, recorded all three nights, and showed a line chart with the correct minutes. But it took an excessive number of tool calls, made repeated invalid calls, and gave confusing updates about approvals and whether the chart was already saved.

- ✓ Created a reusable form for entering a date and minutes.
- ✓ Recorded Nov 18 (25), Nov 19 (15), and Nov 20 (30) without duplicating Nov 20.
- ✓ Displayed a progress chart with all three nights.
- ✗ Made many invalid tool calls and took 229 seconds across 99 runs.
- ✗ Gave inconsistent updates about whether entries were awaiting approval or already recorded.
- ✗ Said to press Save even though the widget tool reported that it had saved the chart.

Cause **slow**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: Make the agent use the exact saved-function names, avoid repeating widget setup, and report clearly whether a form or chart is already saved.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (9 of 99 tool calls failed, had invalid input or got an error or refusal back: database/create_table (failed), database/table_fns_available (invalid-input), database/read_at_instance (invalid-input), widgets/make_widget (invalid-input), hub/fns_search (failed), database/run_query (invalid-input))

6 turns · 99 runs · 64 model calls · hub $0.167 · person $0.0023 · 229s · variant load · ended: satisfied (I now have the reusable nightly form and the progress chart showing all three nights, which is exactly what I asked for.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 1, the assistant had the correct database row-type example and approval guidance, but its first table call failed validation and it tried table operations that reported the table was absent; it also did not ask for the goal or earlier readings needed to answer “how she's doing.” At step 37, the form agent used the unrelated search phrase “trip details,” adding avoidable work. The larger confusion came from the widget helper: at step 47 it said “Saved widgets/reading_minutes_by_date,” while the outer `widgets__make_widget` result described the chart as “Proposed, not saved.” This conflicting state led the assistant at steps 48, 51, and 58 to keep telling the person to press Save, and contributed to making another widget at steps 43 and 53 even though a saved widget reads its source again when run.

- `context:hub/tracking` (0.87): There is no focused workflow for a request to track something over time and evaluate progress. The general guidance says to keep a log and offer a way to add and view entries, but does not prompt for the goal or relevant prior entries when the person asks how someone is doing.
  > ## Tracking something over time
  > When someone wants to track their own data over time, first check whether a saved log or view already fits. If not, a database table is the lasting list of entries; a form is a reusable set of questions for collecting an entry; and a widget is a saved view, such as a chart, over a table-producing function. A form does not store its answers: after the person submits it, use the database functions to save the answers. For a progress request that depends on a target or history, ask for any missing target and the earlier entries they want included; do not invent them. You can set up the reusable entry form while asking, but do not claim the progress view is meaningful until the needed data is present. For example, for a child’s reading log, ask for the nightly-…
- `hub-behaviour` (0.76): Calls that depend on a new table can be sent while creation is awaiting approval or before the table is available, producing “There is no table” invalid-input errors.
  > When a table-creation call is awaiting approval or has not yet completed successfully, do not run table-dependent calls for that table. Queue or defer those calls until creation succeeds; if creation is declined or fails, return a clear message that the dependent calls were not run and why. Do not send them early and return a missing-table validation error.
- `fn-instructions:input/get_input` (0.95): The form agent was given a specific nightly reading-entry request but searched for “trip details,” an unrelated example phrase.
  > When searching for a saved form, use a short phrase that describes the fields in the request you received. Do not copy a phrase from an unrelated example. For example, for a nightly reading entry, search for “reading date and minutes,” not “trip details.” Reuse a form only if its fields actually fit; otherwise continue to the form-writing steps.
- `context:widgets/guide` (0.94): The guidance explains that a saved widget reads its source again when run, but does not explicitly say to refresh an existing widget instead of creating another one when new rows arrive.
  > If a suitable widget is already saved, run that widget to show its current view; it reads its source again, so new database rows appear without making another widget. Use `widgets__make_widget` only when the person wants a new view or a changed widget. For example, after adding earlier reading nights to a log, run the existing reading chart rather than proposing a second chart.
- `hub-behaviour` (0.98): The widget helper’s inner result says `Saved widgets/...`, while the outer result says `Proposed, not saved`; the person and assistant therefore receive conflicting instructions about whether to press Save.
  > Make widget creation return one authoritative save state that matches the stored widget. If the helper has saved a widget, return its saved name and say it is saved; do not also label it “Proposed, not saved” or tell the person to press Save. If the helper has only made a proposal, do not persist it and return a clear proposal state with the Save action. Ensure a repeated call that updates an existing widget reports whether it updated a saved widget or only proposed a change.

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 2: weak 5/10

The assistant created a nightly-entry form, logged the three readings, and ultimately produced a progress chart. But the setup took an excessive number of tool calls with many failures, and the final message said the chart still needed saving even though the run shows it was saved.

- ✓ Created a reusable form for entering a date and minutes.
- ✓ Logged Nov 18–20 with the corrected 2026 date and accurate totals.
- ✓ Was clear that it cannot track reading automatically or send reminders.
- ✗ The form did not automatically write its answers to the log; the assistant had to add the entry separately.
- ✗ Many tool calls failed or used invalid inputs, making the interaction slow and confusing.
- ✗ The final response told the person to save the chart despite a successful widget save in the run.
- ✗ The chart showed all logged dates rather than a selectable weekly view.

Cause **tool-error**, layer **instructions**. Fix: Clarify the widget and database tool argument formats and save-state behavior so the assistant can create the requested view with fewer failed calls and accurately report whether it is saved.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (24 of 171 tool calls failed, had invalid input or got an error or refusal back: database/get_query (invalid-input), database/author_query (invalid-input), widgets/make_widget (invalid-input), database/run_query (invalid-input), hub/fns_search (failed), hub/fns_save (failed), widgets/make_widget (failed), propose (tool-error))

7 turns · 171 runs · 123 model calls · hub $0.297 · person $0.0059 · 515s · variant load · ended: turn-limit (the person had sent 6 follow-ups, the most allowed)

**Diagnosis:** The app already gave the model the right overall pattern in step 1 and, by step 96, a saved query for the requested week. The repeated failures came from two tool-side problems and a later wrong source choice: the widget proposal validator contradicted its schema at steps 78–86 (“unknown key 'description'” even though the schema required it), and the outer widget result at steps 68 and 105 said “Proposed, not saved” despite the nested result saying “Saved widgets/reading_minutes_by_date.” In step 100 the model also sent a slash-form source and a list for `args`, despite the tool instructions specifying tool spelling and an object; it then abandoned the date-range query at steps 101–103 and saved an all-dates chart instead. The inconsistent save result led to the final, incorrect instruction to press Save.

- `tool-description:widgets/make_widget` (0.91): The model repeatedly supplied slash-form source names and, in step 100, a list rather than the required object for `args`, even though the tool schema and examples use tool spelling and an object.
  > For `source`, use the exact name as it appears in the tools, with `/` and `.` written as `__`. For example, use `database__main__reading_minutes_by_date_2`, not `database/main.reading_minutes_by_date_2`. `args` must be one JSON object mapping each required source argument to its value, never a list of key/value pairs. Example: `{"source":"database__main__reading_minutes_by_date_2","request":"Minutes by date for this week","args":{"from":"2026-11-16","to":"2026-11-22"},"show":true}`. Use the source's actual required arguments; if there are none, omit `args`.
- `hub-behaviour` (0.99): The outer widget tool reported “Proposed, not saved” after the nested `offer` result reported that the widget was saved, causing the assistant to tell the person to save an already-saved widget.
  > Make the result returned by `widgets/make_widget` reflect the nested widget run's final state. If `offer` returns `Saved widgets/<name> (version <n>)`, return a saved status and the widget name; do not return “Proposed, not saved.” Return a proposal/not-saved status only when the nested run ended before `offer` saved it. Include the exact final status in the result the chat model receives.

### on (decision models on), rep 3: weak 5/10

It saved all four nights correctly, calculated the average and goal results, and was honest that it could not log automatically. But it never set up a quick input form, and repeated invalid chart attempts meant the user got only a suggestion to change the table’s visualization rather than a ready-to-view chart.

- ✓ Created a persistent reading log and added the dates and minutes accurately.
- ✓ Compared the four recorded nights with the 20-minute goal and correctly excluded the missing night.
- ✓ Clearly explained that nightly logging would still require the user to add entries.
- ✗ Did not provide the requested quick input form; adding entries depended on chat or an exposed function.
- ✗ The chart widget failed repeatedly because its source was supplied in an invalid format.
- ✗ The final visual workaround required the user to find and change visualization options themselves.

Cause **tool-error**, layer **context**. Fix: Use the widget’s required slash-form source name, and provide a simple input form for adding each night’s date and minutes.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (8 of 42 tool calls failed, had invalid input or got an error or refusal back: database/table_fns_available (invalid-input), database/read_at_instance (invalid-input), widgets/make_widget (invalid-input), hub/fns_search (failed))

4 turns · 42 runs · 40 model calls · hub $0.116 · person $0.0025 · 199s · variant on · ended: satisfied (The nightly logging is set up and working, and the assistant was straight that it can't build the chart itself but gave a simple way for me to see the trend.)

**Diagnosis:** The reusable entry form was missed at steps 1 and 25 even though the prompt described `input__get_input`, reusable forms, and using a form for typed fields; the app did not explicitly connect that recurring-form guidance to saving each answer through the database. The chart failures began at step 15 because the widget instructions and examples used `database__...` names while the widget validator required a slash-form qualified source; step 16’s “source: Invalid input” did not explain the format, and the example returned at step 20 reinforced the rejected spelling. Step 17 exposed a similar mismatch between the search tool’s documented tool spelling and its slash-form validator. Later, at steps 31–35, the model fell back to raw rows despite the widget instructions requiring grouped totals for a totals chart, then left the user to change the visualization themselves.

- `context:hub/saved_fns` (0.88): The existing tracking guidance says to provide a way to add entries, but does not give a concrete flow connecting a reusable form to the table’s add function.
  > For a recurring log that needs two or more typed values per entry, make a reusable form as well as the database table. Use the input system’s form maker to ask only for the fields needed for one entry (for example, a reading date and minutes read). A form only collects answers; it does not save them. When the answers arrive, use the table’s add function to save them. Tell the person how to show the saved form again for the next entry. Do not use a form when one quick answer is enough or when the person only wants a log and no repeated entry flow.
- `tool-description:database/table_fns_available` (0.93): The description’s `database__main__...` type example led to an argument rejected as a nonexistent table.
  > Use the table’s plain name in `table` (for example, `reading_minutes`) and pass its database separately when needed (for example, `{"table":"reading_minutes","database":"main"}`). Do not pass the tool spelling `database__main__reading_minutes` as the table name.

items.md:
**Request:** "Keep a list of the books I've read and tell me what I should read next."

**Good:** Starts the list, asks a few books to start from, gives suggestions with reasons.

Mean 6.6/10 · verdicts differ · $0.709

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 1: weak 6/10

The assistant created the list, saved all four books, and gave three relevant suggestions with reasons. But it didn’t preserve the user’s reactions or preferences for future use, didn’t use web for the recommendations, and had several avoidable failed tool calls before completing the task.

- ✓ Asked for books and preferences before making recommendations.
- ✓ Saved all four titles with authors and genres in the database.
- ✓ Suggested three plausible books and explained why each might fit.
- ✗ Did not preserve the user's like/love/OK reactions or preferences in memory.
- ✗ Did not use web to check or ground its recommendations.
- ✗ Made three invalid tool calls and took many steps to finish.

Cause **missed-capability**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: After saving the books, preserve the user’s reactions and stated preferences for future recommendations, use web when useful to verify book details, and avoid the invalid database calls.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (3 of 18 tool calls failed, had invalid input or got an error or refusal back: database/table_fns_available (invalid-input), database/read_at_instance (invalid-input), database/run_query (invalid-input))

2 turns · 18 runs · 11 model calls · hub $0.0429 · person $0.0008 · 74s · variant load · ended: satisfied (The books are saved in the list and I got three good suggestions with reasons, which is exactly what I asked for.)

**Diagnosis:** The assistant handled the main workflow well, but step 3 hit an app inconsistency: `database__table_fns_available` says a table type such as `database__main__expenses` is accepted, yet the call using that form was rejected. At step 7, the model had clear instructions to use `hub__remember` for lasting preferences, but did not do so; it also sent `database__run_query` an array where the tool schema explicitly required an object. The run-query error added confusion by rejecting the `database__main__books_read_create` spelling that the table-fns tool had returned. Finally, the prompt explained web search for current or outside information but did not say to use it to verify details in book recommendations, so the model gave plausible recommendations without web grounding.

- `hub-behaviour` (0.94): `database__table_fns_available` documents that `table` accepts a table type, but rejects the type spelling used in the call.
  > Make `database__table_fns_available` accept both a plain table name (with `database` when needed) and the documented table-type name, such as `database__main__books_read`. If the table cannot be found, return the available table names and say which accepted formats were tried.
- `tool-description:database/run_query` (0.83): The call used an array of key/value pairs for `args`, although the schema requires an object; the instructions should make this easy to distinguish. The function-name spelling returned by table-fns generation was also rejected.
  > For `args`, pass one JSON object whose keys are the saved query's parameter names. Do not pass a list of `{ "key": ..., "value": ... }` objects. Example: `{"fn":"database__main__books_read_create","args":{"title":"Project Hail Mary","author":"Andy Weir"}}`. Use the saved function name exactly as the database tool returned it. If that exact name is rejected, report the naming mismatch rather than suggesting the function does not exist.
- `hub-behaviour` (0.86): `database__run_query` rejected a generated function name in the spelling supplied by `database__table_fns_generate`, making the tools disagree about how to refer to the same saved query.
  > Normalize the tool spelling `database__main__books_read_create` and the qualified spelling `database/main.books_read_create` to the same saved-query name in `database__run_query`. When a name is unknown, return the closest saved query names and the accepted spelling; do not report a generated query as nonexistent solely because of name formatting.
- `context:hub/memory` (0.90): The memory guidance already says to remember lasting preferences, but does not specifically prompt the assistant to preserve recommendation feedback that cannot fit the current table's rating field.
  > When someone shares a lasting preference that will matter in future chats, save it as a user-scoped memory with `hub__remember`. For recommendation tasks, preserve useful feedback as well as broad preferences: for example, that the person loved *Project Hail Mary* and *Educated*, liked *The Midnight Library*, found *Where the Crawdads Sing* just OK, likes science fiction and memoirs, and dislikes long fantasy series. Do not convert words such as “loved” or “just OK” into a numeric score unless the person gives you a scale. A database list and a memory serve different purposes: use the list for entries to look up and memory for preferences that should inform later chats.
- `context:web/basics` (0.82): The web guidance focuses on current or outside information and does not tell the assistant when web checking helps with book recommendations.
  > When recommending specific books, use web search when you need to verify details that support a recommendation, such as an author's name, genre, whether a book is standalone, or whether it is part of a series. **Request:** "When did I last change the furnace filter? I never remember this stuff."

**Good:** Admits it doesn't know yet, offers to start a home-maintenance log, asks for the date.

Mean 6.3/10 · verdicts differ · $0.652

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 1: weak 6/10

It honestly said it couldn’t look up the past change, created a maintenance log with the approximate date and next due date, and clearly explained that it couldn’t send a future reminder. It missed the expected memory save and made two invalid database calls before recovering.

- ✓ Asked for the change date instead of guessing
- ✓ Saved the filter details and estimated next due date in the database
- ✓ Was clear that Google Calendar and future phone nudges weren’t available
- ✓ Distinguished the original February 3 schedule from a date three months after replacing it now
- ✗ Did not use memory to retain the maintenance details
- ✗ Made two invalid database calls and took many steps to complete the log

Cause **missed-capability**, layer **context**. Fix: Save the maintenance details to memory as well as the database, and avoid probing table functions with an invalid table name.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (2 of 21 tool calls failed, had invalid input or got an error or refusal back: database/table_fns_available (invalid-input), database/read_at_instance (invalid-input))

4 turns · 21 runs · 19 model calls · hub $0.0843 · person $0.0016 · 112s · variant load · ended: satisfied (The assistant was honest that it can’t send future nudges, so I’ll use my phone reminder instead.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 3, the assistant overclaimed that no change was recorded in household data even though `database__databases` showed table names and column summaries, not their rows. At step 6, the prompt explicitly presented `database__main__home_maintenance` as an acceptable table identifier, but the lookup rejected it; the assistant recovered by listing tables and using the plain name. At step 11, the prompt already explained that `hub__remember` keeps lasting facts for the person across chats, but the assistant saved the log entry only in the database. It correctly distinguished the original due date from a date three months after a future replacement and accurately explained that no future nudge or Google Calendar event was available.

- `system-prompt` (0.90): The general rule to say only what tool results show did not prevent a broad claim of absence based only on a database table listing.
  > When checking a database, distinguish its table list from its rows. A database listing shows which tables and columns exist; it does not show whether a particular entry exists. Do not say a record is absent unless you queried the relevant rows. If no suitable table is listed or you have not checked the rows, say exactly that and explain that you cannot determine the answer from what you checked.
- `tool-description:database/table_fns_available` (0.93): The description says the `table` argument can be a table type and gives an encoded qualified-name example, but that form was rejected in this call.
  > Use the plain table name in `table`, such as `{"table":"home_maintenance","database":"main"}`. Do not pass the tool-encoded qualified name such as `database__main__home_maintenance`. If you already have the table's plain name and database instance, use those; this tool only lists the table's ready-made functions.
- `context:database/guide` (0.94): The guide says to pass the table as `database__main__chores`, which led to the rejected argument.
  > 3. Call `database__table_fns_available` with the plain table name and its database instance: for example, `{"table":"chores","database":"main"}`. Do not use the tool-encoded name `database__main__chores` as the table value. Then call `database__table_fns_generate` with the same plain table name, the database instance, and the function names returned by the availability call.
- `context:hub/memory` (0.78): The memory instructions describe saving lasting facts, but do not explicitly connect that practice to personally useful details that are also entered into a database log.
  > When someone shares a lasting personal fact they want to be able to recall in future chats, save a short user-scoped memory with `hub__remember`, even if you also save structured details in a database. Keep the database as the detailed log; use memory for a small, salient fact that will help retrieve or use that information later. Do not create a memory for every routine database row, and never suggest that a memory sends reminders or runs by itself.

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 2: weak 6/10

The assistant was honest that it didn’t know the last change date, asked for confirmation, calculated the next due date, and successfully saved the log and memory. It eventually did the right things, but several tool calls failed and the process was unnecessarily long.

- ✓ Did not invent a past filter-change date; checked available notes and explained what it found.
- ✓ Confirmed August 3, 2026 before recording it and calculated November 3, 2026 as the next due date.
- ✓ Successfully saved the maintenance-log entry and a memory.
- ✓ Clearly said it cannot automatically send a reminder or promise to notify the user on app open.
- ✗ Four tool calls failed or had invalid input, including an incorrect database query call that had to be retried.
- ✗ The 29 tool runs and 103 seconds made a straightforward request clumsy and slow.

Cause **tool-error**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: Use the available file and database tools with valid arguments on the first attempt, then save the confirmed change and memory without unnecessary exploratory calls.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (4 of 29 tool calls failed, had invalid input or got an error or refusal back: hub/records_find (failed), hub/resource_read (failed), hub/ctx_search (failed), database/run_query (invalid-input))

3 turns · 29 runs · 32 model calls · hub $0.0655 · person $0.0012 · 103s · variant load · ended: satisfied (I got the next due date and the change was logged and saved as a memory, and the assistant was straight with me that it can't nudge me on its own.)

**Diagnosis:** The main avoidable delay began at step 4: after `hub__data_sets` explicitly returned no stored types, the model searched for record functions and then invented `maintenance/Log` at step 5. It also missed the direct instruction to use `hub__resource_send` when `hub__resource_read` says a resource has no text form (steps 8 and 11), and made an invalid context-name call at step 9; the context search then misleadingly dropped the requested `fs/guide` at step 10. At step 17 it did not follow the prompt’s guidance to offer a reusable log when someone signals they need to keep track of something. Finally, step 24 used a list for `args` even though the tool description says it must be a JSON object. The assistant ultimately confirmed the date, saved the database entry and memory, and accurately described the reminder limitation, but the failed calls and unnecessary detours made a straightforward task take 29 runs.

- `system-prompt` (0.90): The prompt says to use stored types for records and to keep track of things over time, but does not explicitly guard against inventing a record type after an empty `hub__data_sets` result or directly connect a request like “I never remember this stuff” with offering a log.
  > Stored records can only be searched by a type that exists; `hub__records_find` does not create types. First use `hub__data_sets` to see which record types exist. If it returns no types, do not guess a type name or call `hub__records_find`; check relevant files or databases instead. When someone asks about a past event and says they have trouble remembering it, be honest if you find no date, offer to start a reusable log if that would help, and ask what date they think it happened before recording it.
- `hub-behaviour` (0.83): The resource-read error only said the file had no text form, so the next action was not repeated at the point of failure; the model searched for a tool that was already available.
  > When `hub__resource_read` cannot read a resource because it has no text form, include a direct recovery instruction in the result, such as: `This resource has no text form. To view it as-is, call hub__resource_send with the same uri.`
- `tool-description:hub/ctx_search` (0.92): The `names` schema accepts full context names, but the description does not say that a short word such as `guide` is invalid.
  > For `names`, give the full context name, including its system and slash, such as `fs/guide` or `database/guide`; do not give only `guide`. If you do not know the full name, omit `names` and search by words in `text`.
- `hub-behaviour` (0.78): The context decision filter discarded `fs/guide` even though the query explicitly sought the filesystem guide, returning no hits and adding an unnecessary detour.
  > When a context search explicitly names a system and asks for its guide (for example, `systems: ["fs"]` and text asking for the filesystem guide), do not discard that system’s guide solely because the decision model assigns it a low likelihood. Return the matching guide or explain why it is unavailable.
- `tool-description:database/run_query` (0.88): The call supplied `args` as a list of `{key, value}` objects, contrary to the description’s one-object requirement. Generated table functions are also callable directly once loaded, avoiding the extra `run_query` wrapper.
  > For a generated table function, the simplest route is to load the returned function name and call it directly with its named parameters. If you use `database__run_query`, `args` must be one JSON object keyed by those parameter names, never a list of key/value objects. For example, a function with `create(task: text, completed_on: date)` takes `{"fn":"<the exact saved function name>","args":{"task":"Filter change","completed_on":"2026-08-03"}}`.

**Request:** "Can you start keeping track of what I spend on groceries? My last trip was Kroger on Nov 14, $172.48." → "Here's my receipt, add it to what I spent." _[receipt]_

**Good:** Reads the store and total, adds it to the grocery log (seeded in the first step), asks if a category is unclear.

Mean 6.8/10 · verdicts differ · $0.471

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant was transparent that it could not read the image, asked for the missing details, and then correctly recognized that the matching trip was already logged rather than adding it twice. The user had to provide the details, but the trip ended up recorded with the right store, date, and total.

- ✓ Did not pretend to read the receipt or claim a new save.
- ✓ Avoided double-counting the trip already in the log.
- ✓ Confirmed the recorded store, date, and total.
- ✗ Both receipt-reading attempts failed because no OCR or description model was configured.
- ✗ The user had to repeat details that were already in the existing log.

Cause **tool-error**, layer **context**. Fix: Configure an OCR or image-description model for receipt reading, while retaining the fallback of checking whether the trip is already logged.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (2 of 4 tool calls failed, had invalid input or got an error or refusal back: hub/resource_read (failed))

3 turns · 4 runs · 7 model calls · hub $0.0368 · person $0.0007 · 43s · variant load · ended: satisfied (The assistant confirmed the Kroger trip from Nov 14 for $172.48 is already in the grocery spending log, so the receipt's trip is recorded with the right store, date and total.)

**Diagnosis:** The receipt could not be read at steps 4–5 because the tool results explicitly said “no model is set to ocr” and “no model is set to describe,” leaving no working image-reading capability in this run. After that, at step 6, the assistant asked for the date and total even though step 2’s result already established the logged Kroger trip as Nov 14, 2026 for $172.48; it should have asked only whether the receipt matched that entry. The final response correctly used the user’s confirmation and the existing database result to avoid double-counting.

- `hub-behaviour` (0.90): Neither OCR nor image description was configured, so both receipt-reading calls failed with no usable image contents.
  > For deployments that accept image attachments, configure a capable model for both reading text in images (OCR) and describing images. Check that these roles are available before offering image-reading calls; if a role is not configured, tell the chat agent that image reading is unavailable so it can say so and use information already in the conversation rather than retrying an unavailable method.
- `system-prompt` (0.85): The assistant asked the person to repeat the date and amount already present in the conversation and confirmed by a successful database result.
  > Before asking the person for a detail, check the messages and tool results already available in this chat. Do not ask them to repeat a detail those messages or results establish. If an attachment cannot be read, compare the known details with any relevant existing record; ask only for the missing decision (for example, whether a receipt is for a trip already in the grocery log), and do not add a duplicate unless the person confirms it is a separate purchase.

**Request:** "Help me plan my mom's 70th birthday party."

**Good:** Asks the few things that matter (date, how many, budget) in one go, then a plan and a checklist.

Mean 8.6/10 · verdicts differ · $0.147

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 1: pass 9/10

The assistant asked for the key planning details in one go, then provided a practical, personalized checklist and an $800 budget. It also checked memory and found no relevant saved preferences; the plan was presented honestly as suggestions and estimates.

- ✓ Asked for date, guest count, and budget or style together
- ✓ Used Linda’s date, home venue, guest count, budget, and interests in the plan
- ✓ Provided a clear timeline-based checklist and budget breakdown

2 turns · 3 runs · 5 model calls · hub $0.0063 · person $0.0004 · 41s · variant load · ended: satisfied (The assistant gave me the working checklist and budget I asked for, so I have what I need.)

**Diagnosis:** The memory check in step 1 was appropriate and found no relevant saved details. In step 2, the context search returned no items and said the relevant `input/guide` was “dropped” by the decision filter, despite the prompt and `input__get_input` tool already explaining how to ask several typed questions. In step 3, the model therefore chose a plain-text question even though the prompt explicitly says, “Use a form when you need several details.” The question collected the needed information successfully and the final answer was useful and honest, but it skipped the intended form mechanism.

- `hub-behaviour` (0.75): A search for an input guide returned no items and reported that the relevant guide had been dropped by decision filtering, making a fitting guide seem unavailable.
  > When a context search names an exact context item (for example, `input/guide`), return that exact item if it exists and is available; do not let the decision filter drop an exact-name match. If it cannot be loaded, return a clear reason rather than an empty result that suggests no matching guide exists.
- `context:input/basics` (0.85): The model asked several planning questions in plain text even though the input-system guidance says to use a form for multiple details.
  > For an initial planning step that needs two or more separate details from the person, prefer `input__get_input` so they can answer in one form. Ask only the few essentials needed for a useful first response; do not collect every possible preference. For example, for an event plan you might ask for the date, approximate guest count, and budget or style together. After showing the form, end your turn and wait for the person's answers. Use a plain-text question for a quick, simple question, not as a substitute for a multi-field form.

> ## Party checklist
> 
> ### This week
> - [ ] Choose a start and end time; a 3–4 hour afternoon or early-evening gathering could work well.
> - [ ] Make a guest list and send invitations. Ask guests to RSVP by **January 2** and mention any dietary restrictions.
> - [ ] Check that you’ll have enough seating, table space, and serving dishes for 30.
> - [ ] Decide whether you’ll cook, order some food, or ask a few people to bring something.
> 
> ### By December 5
> - [ ] Set the menu. One manageable Italian buffet idea:
>   - Antipasti or a simple appetizer
>   - Two pasta options, including one vegetarian
>   - Salad and bread
>   - Cake, plus coffee or tea
> - [ ] Pick a cake and decide whether you’ll bake or order it.
> - [ ] Choose a gardening-inspired touch: potted herbs for the table, seed-packet place cards, or a small plant for each guest to take home.
> - [ ] Check kitchen equipment, chairs, plates, glasses, and serving utensils; borrow or rent anything missing.
> 
> ### By December 19
> - [ ] Confirm food plans and order anything that needs advance notice.
> - [ ] Plan a toast, short slideshow, or “70 memories and wishes” cards—whichever feels most like Linda.
> - [ ] Make a playlist of music she loves.
> - [ ] Decide who can help with setup, serving, and cleanup.
> 
> ### By January 2
> - [ ] Follow up with anyone who hasn’t RSVP’d; update the headcount.
> - [ ] Finalize food quantities and check allergies or dietary needs.
> - [ ] Buy shelf-stable drinks, pantry items, candles, and decorations.
> - [ ] Sketch a simple room layout, including a clear path to the bathroom and a place for coats.
> 
> ### The week of the party
> - [ ] Confirm food pickup or helper plans.
> - [ ] Shop for fresh ingredients and flowers or herbs.
> - [ ] Prepare anything that can be made ahead, such as sauce, décor, or memory cards.
> - [ ] Tidy the guest areas and make a bad-weather plan for arrivals and parking.
> 
> ### Friday, January 15
> - [ ] Set up tables, chairs, decorations, and serving areas.
> - [ ] Chill drinks and prep food that can be made ahead.
> - [ ] Put out labels for dishes, especially vegetarian or allergy-conscious options.
> - [ ] Charge your phone and set aside a spot for gifts and cards.
> 
> ### Saturday, January 16
> - [ ] Finish cooking and set out food safely.
> - [ ] Put on the playlist and welcome guests.
> - [ ] Make time for the toast or memory activity.
> - [ ] Take a few family photos with Linda.
> 
> ## A sample $800 budget
> 
> | Category | Budget |
> |---|---:|
> | Main meal and sides | $400 |
> | Cake and dessert | $100 |
> | Drinks, coffee, and tea | $100 |
> | Gardening-themed decorations or small favors | $80 |
> | Ice, serving supplies, and other essentials | $60 |
> | Cushion for unexpected costs | $60 |
> | **Total** | **$800** |
> 
> These are planning targets, not quoted prices; cooking more at home or asking a couple of guests to bring a dish could leave more room for the cake or keepsakes.

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 2: pass 8/10

The assistant gathered the key planning details in one form, then produced a tailored party plan and a detailed week-by-week checklist with peanut-allergy precautions. It initially saved the checklist to a file the user couldn’t find, but promptly provided the full checklist in chat.

- ✓ Asked for date, area, guest count, budget, and preferences in one form.
- ✓ Tailored the plan to the gardening theme, Italian food, budget, and allergy concerns.
- ✓ Provided a practical, tickable checklist with allergy steps throughout.
- ✗ The checklist was first saved to a file the user couldn’t access on their phone.

4 turns · 11 runs · 17 model calls · hub $0.0195 · person $0.0017 · 96s · variant load · ended: satisfied (The full week-by-week checklist with tick boxes and peanut-allergy steps is now in the chat, which is what I asked for.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 1 the model skipped the explicit Memory instruction to search before asking about personal details, and at step 12 it did not apply the instruction to remember useful lasting facts the person shared. The checklist failure began at step 13: although the prompt describes `fs` as working in folders on the person’s machine, it does not clearly say to prefer an in-chat checklist unless a file is requested or to warn that a local file may not be available on a phone. The model therefore wrote a file at step 14 and gave only its path at step 15. That step’s `created: true` result confirms a file was created, but not its contents; the prompt also says not to describe a file that has not been read. Step 16 recovered by putting the complete checklist in chat.

- `context:hub/memory` (0.83): The existing Memory guidance says to search before asking for personal details and to remember lasting facts, but the model skipped both actions in this conversation.
  > ## Memory: before asking and after learning
  > Before asking the person for personal information, search memories for relevant facts or preferences first (`hub__ctx_search` with `origins: ["memory"]`). If no relevant memory is found, ask only for what the task needs. After the person shares information, use `hub__remember` for separate facts or preferences that are likely to matter in future chats. Do not save one-time plans, dates, or budgets as lasting memories unless the person asks you to. Use `scope: "user"` for a lasting fact about this person; use `scope: "session"` for a fact useful only in this chat. Never claim to have remembered something unless the tool result confirms it.
- `context:fs/guide` (0.88): The file guidance explains how to save a document, but does not establish that an ordinary request for a checklist should be answered in chat first, nor that a file in the machine’s served folders may not be accessible on a phone. It also does not require checking the saved content before describing it.
  > Use a file only when the person asks for a file or confirms they want one. If they ask for a checklist or list to use in chat, provide it directly in the chat with Markdown checkboxes; do not default to saving a file. Files are stored in folders served from the machine and may not be available on the person’s other devices; never imply that a file is synced or accessible on a phone unless a result confirms that. After `fs__write`, use `fs__read` before describing the file’s contents. The write result can confirm that a file was created, but it does not verify what the file contains.

**Request:** "What's going on this weekend near me?"

**Good:** Uses or asks for the location, real events with dates and links.

Mean 7.2/10 · verdicts differ · $0.177

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 1: pass 8/10

Asked for the missing location and clarified which weekend, then provided several family-friendly Columbus-area options with dates, times, prices where available, and links. The options were researched from event pages and the assistant was clear that they were Columbus-area picks, not specifically Clintonville events.

- ✓ Asked for location and resolved the ambiguous timing before searching.
- ✓ Provided multiple relevant, dated options with links, including official event pages.
- ✓ Tailored the suggestions to children ages 8 and 6 and noted reservation or admission details.
- ✗ The research took 62 tool calls and 91 seconds, more than needed for this request.

2 turns · 62 runs · 12 model calls · hub $0.0134 · person $0.0004 · 91s · variant load · ended: satisfied (I got several family-friendly options for next weekend with dates, times, prices, and links, which is exactly what I asked for.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 1, the prompt already said to search memory before asking for a personal detail, but the model asked for the location without doing so; at step 2 it also failed to preserve the location and family preference in memory after they were supplied. The major inefficiency followed at steps 2–11: although the web guide said to read the best “one or two pages,” the model pursued a “comprehensive guide,” used advanced searches immediately, and repeatedly chased Community Day results whose search summaries conflicted with the event pages it had read. Those mismatches in the search results encouraged more investigation, but the model should have excluded the disputed event and stopped once it had enough verified options. Finally, step 12 added specific Aglow and Wildlights attractions not established by the displayed tool results, despite the system instruction to say only what tool results show.

- `system-prompt` (0.82): The prompt says, “Do the same before you ask for a personal detail,” and to remember lasting facts or preferences, but the model neither searched for a remembered location nor saved the location and family preference after the person supplied them.
  > For requests such as “near me,” check memory for the person's relevant location before asking where they are. If no relevant memory is found, ask for the location. When a person volunteers a lasting location or preference that is useful in future chats, save it with hub__remember at user scope, unless they indicate it is temporary or do not want it remembered. For example, a person's neighborhood and preference for family-friendly outings can help with later local recommendations.
- `context:web/guide` (0.90): The guide says “Pick the one or two best results” and read those pages, but does not give a clear stopping rule or discourage repeated searches when event dates conflict.
  > For a local-events request, start with one focused basic search. Read the best one or two relevant pages, preferring official event pages. If the person asks for a few options, stop when you have a few suitable events with dates confirmed on pages you read; do not keep searching for a comprehensive calendar. If a search summary conflicts with a page you read, trust the page and exclude that event unless one focused search finds an official page confirming the requested date. Use an advanced search only when the basic search did not find enough useful results.
- `hub-behaviour` (0.68): Search results included an October 30–November 1 page for a November 28–29 request, and search summaries described museum events on November 29 while the read event pages showed November 1 or November 2.
  > Improve web search ranking and result summaries for date-specific event queries: prioritize pages whose event dates match the requested dates, distinguish a page's publication date from the event date, and avoid presenting an event date in the answer summary unless it is supported by a result that matches the requested date. When a result page's title or event date conflicts with the query dates, rank it lower or flag the mismatch.
- `system-prompt` (0.86): The existing evidence rule says, “Say only what your tool results show,” but the final response included specific attractions not supported by the displayed results.
  > For current events, include a specific attraction, activity, time, price, or admission detail only when it appears in a tool result you received. A search snippet or summary can suggest an event, but do not add details from memory or assumption. If a page result is cut off or does not show a detail, omit that detail or say you could not confirm it.

The assistant asked for location, gave a clear “it depends” answer with relevant reasons and real sources, and suggested a useful next step. But it took 52 tool runs and 82 seconds to get there, including a failed page read that it worked around.

- ✗ Used far more research steps than this request needed.
- ✗ One web page read failed, though the assistant recovered.

Cause **slow**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: Set a tighter research budget: use a few authoritative sources, recover from a failed page with one alternative, and answer once the evidence supports a useful recommendation.

2 turns · 52 runs · 13 model calls · hub $0.0151 · person $0.0007 · 82s · variant load · ended: satisfied (The assistant gave a clear 'it depends' verdict with reasons, a practical next step, and real sources, which is exactly what I asked for.)

**Diagnosis:** The research expanded far beyond what the user needed despite the web guide’s instruction to “Pick the one or two best results,” and the prompt’s general instruction not to spend steps on unnecessary calls. After the failed read of a guessed DOE URL at step 8, step 9 added four more searches instead of using one alternative and stopping. The final recommendation was useful, but step 13 attached an ENERGY STAR claim to a page the model had not verified for that claim; the search result itself cautioned that the visible criteria were not specific to residential equipment. The result was a sound answer delivered with unnecessary research time and one failed call.

- `context:web/guide` (0.88): The guide says to select “the one or two best results,” but does not set an overall research budget or make stopping after one failed read concrete enough to prevent repeated searches.
  > For an ordinary recommendation or comparison, use a small research budget: make at most 3 searches and read at most 4 pages total. Prefer official or otherwise authoritative sources, and select pages that answer the main decision rather than researching every related detail. Stop when the evidence supports a useful, qualified answer. If a page read fails, try one relevant alternative result from a search you already made; do not start a new round of searches unless no suitable alternative exists. If something remains unconfirmed, say so instead of continuing to research.
- `context:web/guide` (0.91): The guide says to answer from pages read and cite their URLs, but does not explicitly require checking that the cited page supports the particular claim. This allowed a guessed URL and a citation whose read text did not establish the claim.
  > Before reading a page, use a URL from a search result, the person, or a page you have read; do not guess a URL. Before citing a page for a factual claim, check that the text returned by `web__read` actually supports that claim. Search snippets are for finding pages, not proof. Do not cite a page for a detail it does not establish. For a conclusion you infer from general information (for example, whether a technology is suitable in a particular city), label it as an inference and say what local detail you could not confirm.

**Agent**:
> ## Verdict: **It depends—but it’s worth getting quotes, especially for a dual-fuel system.**
> 
> Your **15-year-old AC** makes this a good time to compare a heat pump with a standard AC replacement. A heat pump can provide both cooling and heating, while your **12-year-old gas furnace** could stay in place as backup for the coldest weather. I wouldn’t replace a working furnace early *just to save money on gas* without comparing the actual quotes and your bills.
> 
> **Why it could make sense:** Cold-climate heat pumps are designed to heat in cold weather, and Columbus is within the range where they’re a practical option. ENERGY STAR’s “cold climate” designation requires tested low-temperature performance. For your house, ask for a **dual-fuel quote** and a **room-by-room heat-loss calculation**—not a system sized just from the old AC.
> 
> **Why the savings aren’t a sure thing:** You already have natural gas, and the cost comparison depends on your actual electricity rate, gas delivery charges, equipment efficiency and how the system is controlled. Columbia Gas’s November 2026 SCO price is **$0.5067/Ccf for gas supply**; that’s not your full gas bill, and it can change monthly. Without your bills and contractor prices, I can’t say whether the heat pump will pay back.
> 
> **In short:** If you’re replacing the AC anyway, get a heat-pump/dual-fuel quote alongside a regular AC quote. Keep the furnace unless a full replacement makes sense on price, condition, or comfort—not on assumed energy savings alone. Also, don’t count on a federal heat-pump tax credit for an installation completed in 2026; the IRS says the credit doesn’t apply to equipment placed in service after Dec. 31, 2025. Ohio’s rebate page describes state programs, but confirm current availability before factoring any rebate into your budget.
> 
> **Sources**
> - [U.S. Department of Energy: Cold-climate air-source heat pumps](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/articles/cold-climate-air-source-heat-pumps-innovative-technology-stay-warm-winter)
> - [ENERGY STAR: Heat pump specification](https://www.energystar.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/HP%20Version%206.2%20Specification%20Revised%20February%202026_0.pdf)

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 2: pass 8/10

The assistant asked for the location, used Columbus-specific research and gave a clear, appropriately qualified recommendation tied to the aging AC and existing furnace. It cited relevant sources and offered a practical apples-to-apples next step without claiming guaranteed savings.

- ✓ Asked for location before giving location-dependent advice.
- ✓ Gave a direct “worth getting a quote, but don’t assume savings” answer.
- ✓ Explained dual-fuel and comparing the heat pump against AC replacement.
- ✓ Cited sources and was clear about the limits of cost estimates.
- ✗ One attempted ENERGY STAR page returned 404; the extra research also made the run longer than needed.

Cause **tool-error**, layer **fn**. Fix: Skip or replace the dead ENERGY STAR URL and stop researching once reliable sources support the recommendation.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (1 of 40 tool calls failed, had invalid input or got an error or refusal back: web/read (failed))

2 turns · 40 runs · 12 model calls · hub $0.0124 · person $0.0004 · 82s · variant load · ended: satisfied (It gave me the it-depends answer I wanted, with the reasons that matter to me (dual-fuel, compare against AC replacement, running costs) and real sources.)

**Diagnosis:** The response was broadly useful, but the research path was longer than needed: at steps 5–10 the model used advanced and repeated searches, including a Columbus climate search whose result was about Independence Day rather than heating conditions. The web guide already said to pick the best one or two results and read them. At step 3 the model itself noticed the furnace fuel needed checking, but did not ask; at step 12 it consequently stated that the person had a gas furnace without evidence. The final answer also gave a specific gas price not visible in the read page and linked the tax-credit claim to an IRS page whose read text did not substantiate it. Step 11’s attempted ENERGY STAR read failed with a 404.

- `system-prompt` (0.91): The prompt says, “When a detail is missing… Never fill it in yourself,” but the model noticed the missing heating fuel and still called the furnace gas.
  > For advice whose answer depends on a person’s home or equipment, do not infer missing facts from a partial description. For example, “furnace” does not tell you whether the fuel is gas, electricity, or something else. Ask for the missing essential detail before making a comparison that depends on it; otherwise state the uncertainty and keep the recommendation conditional.
- `context:web/guide` (0.87): The guide recommends reading one or two best results, but does not give a clear stopping rule for a multi-factor advice question; the model continued searching after it had useful local calculator information.
  > For advice that depends on several factors, research only the factors needed for a useful first answer. Start with a basic search; use advanced search only if basic results do not find adequate sources. Usually one relevant local source and one authoritative source are enough for a qualified recommendation. Stop when those sources support the main conclusion. Ask the person for missing personal inputs rather than searching for a precision the available information cannot provide. If you need a price, date, or policy detail, read the page and verify that exact detail in its text before stating it. If a page is empty or returns an error, use a different working result or say you could not confirm the detail; do not treat the failed page as evidence.
- `hub-behaviour` (0.62): A web search result led to an ENERGY STAR URL that returned `404 Not Found`, producing a failed run.
  > When web search results include a URL that the web reader has recently confirmed returns 404, suppress that result or mark it unavailable so the model can choose a working result instead.
- `system-prompt` (0.90): The general rule to “Name where a fact came from” did not prevent a specific price and tax-credit claim from being paired with pages whose read text did not show those details.
  > For a factual claim that you present as checked against a source, make sure the page you cite was successfully read and its text supports that exact claim. A search snippet or search-generated summary is not confirmation that the cited page says it. If the page is unreadable, empty, or does not contain the detail, say you could not confirm it or leave the detail out.

> 
> **Bottom line:** *Yes* if you’re replacing equipment anyway or leaving electric resistance/propane/oil heat. *It depends* if you’re replacing a working gas furnace—get a side-by-side estimate using your actual bills and the full electric rate.   > For advice or recommendations that depend on the person's circumstances, first check whether you know the key facts that could change the conclusion. Ask for missing facts before researching toward a firm recommendation, or state that the result is provisional and identify what is unknown. For example, a heat-pump recommendation may depend on the location, current heating and cooling equipment and its age. Do not assume those facts from local research. Then research the general and location-specific evidence, read the pages you rely on, and cite their URLs.

items.md:
**Request:** "Help me write a nice note to my neighbor about their dog barking."

**Good:** A friendly draft, offers a firmer one; no tools needed.

Mean 8.1/10 · same verdict every rep · $0.0554

### load (decision models on, loading what they pick), rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant produced a short, warm note tailored to Dave, Bruno, the barking hours, and Alex and Sara’s names. It didn’t offer a firmer alternative as the Good line requested, but the final note was ready to leave on the door.

- ✓ Used the details the person provided without needing tools
- ✓ Kept the wording friendly and softened it when asked
- ✓ Asked for the sign-off names rather than guessing
- ✗ Did not offer a firmer version

4 turns · 0 runs · 4 model calls · hub $0.0098 · person $0.0007 · 33s · variant load · ended: satisfied (The note is short, warm, and friendly, and it's signed Alex & Sara, so it's ready to print and leave on Dave's door.)

**Diagnosis:** The model correctly needed no tools, and the person's later details supported the names, dog, location and barking hours. However, at step 1 it invented “quite a bit lately” and a possibility about the neighbor's awareness; at step 4 it again put an unprovided belief in the senders' voice. The prompt says not to fill in missing details, but its examples focus on amounts, dates, sizes, names and counts rather than invented personal experiences or beliefs. The expected firmer option was absent from both the person's request and the model's prompt, so its omission was not a model error. At step 3 the prompt did explicitly say to do the parts independent of a missing detail, yet the model only asked for names instead of also revising the note.

- `system-prompt` (0.90): The general instruction not to invent details does not explicitly warn against writing unprovided experiences, frequency or beliefs in a message on the person's behalf.
  > When drafting words for the person to send, do not invent their experiences, frequency estimates, intentions or beliefs, or another person's knowledge or motives. Use only details the person gave you. If a useful detail is unknown, omit it, use a clear placeholder, or ask; prefer neutral wording over putting an unsupported thought in the sender's voice.
- `system-prompt` (0.76): Nothing in the prompt asks the model to offer a firmer alternative when drafting a tactful note about a complaint or request, though the Good line expects one here.
  > For a personal message about a delicate request or complaint, give the requested draft first. When a nearby tone option would be useful, briefly offer one optional alternative, such as a slightly firmer version of a friendly note. Do not add tone variants mechanically to unrelated writing requests or overwhelm the person with choices.
- `system-prompt` (0.88): The instruction to do independent parts when information is missing was not followed: the model asked for the sign-off names but did not revise the note.
  > When you must ask for a missing detail, first complete any useful part that does not depend on it. For example, if names are missing from a requested sign-off, provide the revised message with a sign-off placeholder and ask for the names in the same reply; do not only promise to revise it later.

You may save the recipe while waiting, but do not present the shopping list as tailored or complete until you have their answer. For example, if they say they have pasta, salt, pepper, and olive oil, leave those off the list of items to buy.
